explain.summary: Swallowing isn't water falling into Leila's stomach. Once she swallows, rings of muscle along her 25-cm food tube squeeze one after another, pushing the water ahead of them — like toothpaste squeezed along a tube. Gravity only helps a little when she's upright. So upside down the water still arrives; it just takes a few seconds longer, especially for thick drinks.
rules: The muscle wave delivers the sip whichever way up she is.
Gravity's help goes from full (standing) to none (lying) to working against her (handstand).
Each sip takes about 6 seconds upright and a few seconds longer lying down or upside down; thick drinks take longer.
Big gulps upside down lose a little; with the squeeze switched off, only gravity would work — and upside down it would fail.

source.fact: Once you begin swallowing it becomes automatic; peristalsis pushes food down the esophagus — the muscle behind the food squeezes while the muscle ahead relaxes.
Swallowing does not depend on gravity: people swallow lying down and astronauts eat and drink in orbit; on Earth gravity gives only subtle help.
In a study, food took longer to travel down the esophagus lying down than sitting; sitting, a thick paste took about 7.5 s and a liquid about 6.1 s.
The esophagus is a muscular tube about 25 cm (10 inches) long.

choice.what: Upside-down times are extended from the lying-down numbers
choice.why: The study measured sitting and lying, not handstands; we continued the same trend.

choice.what: Tilt changes gravity's help in a straight line
choice.why: Real help follows the angle more smoothly; a straight line keeps the dial simple.

choice.what: The food tube is scaled with height
choice.why: Tube length roughly follows body size; 25 cm is the adult figure.

choice.what: Switching the squeeze off is imaginary
choice.why: It lets you test hypothesis C: if gravity did the work, upside-down sips would never arrive.

illustrative: Leila's height, her sip sizes and the small loss for big upside-down gulps are made up for a fictional story.

citations.title: Your Digestive System & How It Works
citations.supports: Once you begin swallowing the process becomes automatic; peristalsis pushes food down the esophagus to the stomach — the muscle behind the food squeezes while the muscle ahead relaxes.

citations.title: Spaceflight could change how astronauts swallow, eat and drink in subtle ways
citations.supports: A swallowing researcher explains that swallowing does not depend on gravity — people swallow lying down and astronauts eat and drink in orbit; on Earth gravity gives only subtle assistance; each swallow uses more than 30 muscles.

citations.title: Effect of swallowed bolus viscosity and body position on esophageal transit, contraction and perception of transit (Arquivos de Gastroenterologia)
citations.supports: Esophageal transit was longer lying down (supine) than sitting; sitting, a thick paste took longer than a liquid (about 7.5 s vs 6.1 s); lying down both took about 8 s.

citations.title: Anatomy of the Esophagus
citations.supports: The esophagus is a muscular tube about ten inches (25 cm) long running from the throat to the stomach.

limits.text: This is a simplified learning model. Real people vary with age, fitness and health. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of any real person.
limits.wellbeing: Eat and drink sitting up in everyday life; if swallowing ever hurts or feels stuck, tell an adult.
